introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0780 Physics 1, June 2024, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Calculators are allowed.

**Constants used in the answers** (the paper itself prints no data sheet): permittivity of free space $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$; permeability of free space $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$; elementary charge $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$; Planck constant $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$; speed of light $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; Boltzmann constant $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; molar gas constant $R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; acceleration of free fall $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; Coulomb constant $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Section I (thirty five questions), Questions 1-35.** Directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements in this section is followed by four suggested answers. Select the best answer in each case.

**Section II (ten questions), Multiple Selection, Questions 36-45.** Directions: Each question or incomplete statement in this section is followed by three numbered responses. One or two of the responses may be correct. CHOOSE: A - if 1 and 2 are correct; B - if 2 and 3 are correct; C - if 1 only is correct; D - if 3 only is correct. (Directions summarised: A = 1, 2 only; B = 2, 3 only; C = 1 only; D = 3 only.)

**Section III (five questions), Questions 46-50.** Direction: Each of the questions (46-50) has four sets of graphs A - D. Which of the graphs in each question best fits the relationship between $x$ and $y$?

questions.enonce_markdown: The base unit of magnetic field intensity is
questions.corrige_markdown: The quantity meant here is the magnetic flux density $B$, whose unit is the tesla. From $F = BIl$ we get $B = \dfrac{F}{Il}$, so $\mathrm{T} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{A\,m}} = \mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$. Option A is the weber (flux, $\mathrm{T\,m^2}$); options B and D are not units of $B$. (Read literally, "field intensity" $H$ would be in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, which is not among the options, so $B$ is intended.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The back of the hand feels cold when some alcohol is dropped on it because
questions.corrige_markdown: Alcohol is volatile and evaporates quickly. To change from liquid to vapour it needs latent heat of vaporization, which it takes from the skin of the hand. The hand loses energy and feels cold. Alcohol is at room temperature (option A is false), and heat capacity does not explain a cooling by evaporation (B and C). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: alcohol is at a lower temperature than the atmosphere
alcohol has a larger heat capacity than your body
alcohol has a lower heat capacity than your body
alcohol extracts latent heat of vaporization from the hand.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pairs both make use of critical damping?
questions.corrige_markdown: Critical damping brings a system back to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. A moving-coil galvanometer needle is critically damped so that it settles quickly on the reading, and a car shock absorber is designed to be (nearly) critically damped so that the car does not bounce. A simple pendulum is lightly damped, and house foundations and bridges are not damped devices of this kind. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Galvanometer and shock absorber in cars
House foundations and shock absorbers in cars

questions.enonce_markdown: The area under a force ($F$) against time ($t$) graph for a moving object is the;
questions.corrige_markdown: The area under an $F$-$t$ graph is $\int F\,\mathrm{d}t$, the impulse of the force. By Newton's second law, $F = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}$, so $\int F\,\mathrm{d}t = \Delta p$: the change in linear momentum. (Work is the area under an $F$-$x$ graph.) **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: change in linear momentum of the object
total distance covered by the object

questions.enonce_markdown:
The resultant force acting on object O in figure 1 is;

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Take east as $+x$ and north as $+y$. The $80\ \mathrm{N}$ force makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, so its components are $80\cos30^\circ = 69.3\ \mathrm{N}$ east and $80\sin30^\circ = 40\ \mathrm{N}$ north. The $50\ \mathrm{N}$ force points west. Then $R_x = 69.3 - 50 = 19.3\ \mathrm{N}$ and $R_y = 40\ \mathrm{N}$. $R = \sqrt{19.3^2 + 40^2} = 44.4\ \mathrm{N} \approx 44\ \mathrm{N}$, at $\tan^{-1}(40/19.3) = 64^\circ$ above east, which is north-east of O. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The strings of a nylon guitar of cross-sectional area $0.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ store elastic potential energy of $0.8\ \mathrm{J}$ when stretched by $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. If Young's modulus for nylon is $2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, then the length of the string is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Elastic energy $U = \tfrac12 k x^2$ with $k = \dfrac{YA}{L}$. So $U = \dfrac{YAx^2}{2L}$ and $$L = \frac{YAx^2}{2U} = \frac{(2\times10^{9})(0.5\times10^{-6})(0.020)^2}{2\times0.8} = \frac{0.40}{1.6} = 0.25\ \mathrm{m} = 25.0\ \mathrm{cm}.$$ **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Platinum resistance thermometers are quite sensitive because;
questions.corrige_markdown: Sensitivity means a large change in resistance for a small change in temperature, which is what a high temperature coefficient of resistance gives ($R_\theta = R_0(1+\alpha\theta)$ with a large $\alpha$). A high melting point gives a wide range, not sensitivity, and a low heat capacity would affect response time. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: platinum has a high temperature coefficient of resistance
the thermometers have relatively low heat capacities
platinum has a high melting point
the thermometers have relatively high heat capacities

questions.enonce_markdown: A sample of gas has a root mean square (rms) speed of $2.2\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at STP. What is the value of its rms speed at $80\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pressure of one atmosphere?
questions.corrige_markdown: STP is $273\ \mathrm{K}$ and one atmosphere, and $c_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}\propto\sqrt{T}$ (the pressure does not enter at fixed $T$). With $T = 273 + 80 = 353\ \mathrm{K}$: $$c_{rms} = 2.2\times10^{3}\sqrt{\frac{353}{273}} = 2.2\times10^{3}\times1.137 = 2.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$ Pitfall: using Celsius temperatures (ratio $80/0$) or forgetting the square root. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 shows a graph of stopping potential $V_s$ plotted against frequency, $f$, for nichrome.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

Which of the following is **CORRECT**?
questions.corrige_markdown: Einstein: $eV_s = hf - \phi$, so $V_s = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$. The gradient is $\dfrac{h}{e}$ (not $h$: option D is wrong). The intercept on the vertical axis is $-\dfrac{\phi}{e}$, a potential, not the work function (B is wrong). The intercept on the horizontal axis is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$. Hence $$\text{gradient}\times f_0\times e = \frac{h}{e}\times\frac{\phi}{h}\times e = \phi.$$ Option C omits the factor $e$ and gives $\phi/e$ (in volts). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The product of gradient of the graph, the value of the intercept on the horizontal axis and the electronic charge, is the work function for nichrome.
The value of the intercept on the vertical axis is the work function for nichrome.
The product of gradient of the graph and the value of the intercept on the horizontal axis, is the work function for nichrome.
The gradient of the graph is the Planck's constant

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3a shows a spring of spring constant $K$ extended by a mass $m$. In figure 3b two identical springs connected as shown are extended by the same mass $m$ attached to the middle of a short connecting bar.

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

If both systems are set into oscillation, which of the following is true?
questions.corrige_markdown: In figure 3b both springs hang from the support and share the load, so they are in parallel: the combined spring constant is $2K$ (twice that of 3a, so C is false). Each spring carries $mg/2$, so the extension is half that of 3a (D is false). The frequency $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}$ is $\sqrt2$ times larger, so the period is shorter (B is false) and the mass oscillates faster. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Mass, m, oscillates faster in figure 3b than in 3a
Mass, m, has a longer period of oscillation in figure 3b than in 3a
The combined spring constant for the system in 3b is half that in 3a
Mass, m, extends the combined springs in 3b twice as much as the single spring in 3a

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the decay constant for Co-60 is 0.132. Its half-life is:
questions.corrige_markdown: $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.132} = 5.25$ years (the unit of $\lambda$, $\mathrm{year^{-1}}$, is not printed but is implied by the options). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two parallel plates each of area $0.04\ \mathrm{m^2}$ placed $5\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart in a vacuum as shown in figure 4,

![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

The potential of the upper plate is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The lower plate is earthed ($0\ \mathrm{V}$), so the potential of the upper plate is the p.d. across the capacitor, $V = Q/C$. With $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.04)}{5\times10^{-3}} = 7.08\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}$ and $Q = 0.02\ \mu\mathrm{C} = 2\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{C}$: $$V = \frac{2\times10^{-8}}{7.08\times10^{-11}} = 282\ \mathrm{V}.$$ **Answer: D.**

Force between two long parallel currents over a length $l$: $F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2 l}{2\pi d}$. With $l = 200\ \mathrm{cm} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $d = 2.0\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.020\ \mathrm{m}$: $$I^2 = \frac{2\pi d F}{\mu_0 l} = \frac{1.6\times10^{-6}\times0.020}{2\times10^{-7}\times2.0} = 0.080\ \mathrm{A^2}, \qquad I = 0.28\ \mathrm{A}\approx 0.3\ \mathrm{A}.$$ Pitfall: $0.08$ (option A) is $I^2$, not $I$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 6 represents a cyclic thermodynamic process. If the heat supplied is $\mathrm{d}Q$ and the change in internal energy is $\mathrm{d}U$, the quantity of heat supplied to the system is given by:

![fig-6](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: First law: $\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}U + \mathrm{d}W$, where $\mathrm{d}W$ is the net work done by the gas. In a cycle on a $P$-$V$ diagram the net work done equals the area enclosed by the loop, here $A = (P_1-P_0)(V_2-V_1)$. So $\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}U + A$ (and, for a complete cycle, $\mathrm{d}U = 0$, so $Q = A$). Options B, C and D multiply the area by a pressure or a volume, which gives wrong dimensions. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figures 7 a and 7 b show the arrangement of bulbs each with resistance as shown.

![fig-7](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

Which of the following is true?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Figure 7a:** the $10\ \Omega$ resistor and the two $10\ \Omega$ bulbs are in series, $R = 30\ \Omega$, $I = \dfrac{24}{30} = 0.80\ \mathrm{A}$ through each bulb, power per bulb $I^2R = 0.80^2\times10 = 6.4\ \mathrm{W}$.

**Figure 7b:** the two bulbs are in parallel ($5\ \Omega$) and in series with the $10\ \Omega$ resistor, $R = 15\ \Omega$, battery current $I = \dfrac{24}{15} = 1.6\ \mathrm{A}$, split equally: $0.80\ \mathrm{A}$ in each bulb, power per bulb $0.80^2\times10 = 6.4\ \mathrm{W}$.

All four bulbs therefore have the same brightness. The battery in 7b supplies twice the current ($1.6\ \mathrm{A}$ against $0.80\ \mathrm{A}$), so its charge runs out in half the time: it runs down faster. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The brightness of the bulbs in figure 7b is the same but more than those in 7a
The brightness of all four bulbs is the same but battery in 7b will run down faster
The brightness of the bulbs in figure 7a is same but more than that in 7b
The brightness of all four bulbs is the same and both batteries will last for the same length of time.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 shows the energy-level diagram for the electron in the hydrogen atom.

![fig-8](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

When the electron in the hydrogen atom makes a transition from energy level $n=4$ to the ground state $n = 1$, it emits light of frequency
questions.corrige_markdown: The photon energy is $\Delta E = E_4 - E_1 = -0.85 - (-13.60) = 12.75\ \mathrm{eV} = 12.75\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 2.04\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}$. Then $$f = \frac{\Delta E}{h} = \frac{2.04\times10^{-18}}{6.63\times10^{-34}} = 3.1\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: N-type semiconductors are more widely applicable in electronic devices than P-type because
questions.corrige_markdown: In an n-type semiconductor the majority carriers are electrons; in a p-type they are holes. Electrons have a higher mobility than holes (a hole moves by electrons hopping from atom to atom), so n-type material gives faster devices with lower resistance. Both types are electrically neutral overall (A is false), and the other options are not the physical reason. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the net charge in the N-type is electrons
N-type are easier to manufacture than P-type
the N-type are more compact than the P-type.

questions.enonce_markdown: An object A, of mass $3.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest by a net force of $5\ \mathrm{N}$ in $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Another object, B, of mass $2.8\ \mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest by the same force in $1.6\ \mathrm{s}$. The ratio of the gain in kinetic energy of A to that of B is
questions.corrige_markdown: From rest, $Ft = mv$, so $E_k = \dfrac{(mv)^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(Ft)^2}{2m}$. For A: $\dfrac{(5\times2.0)^2}{2\times3.5} = 14.29\ \mathrm{J}$. For B: $\dfrac{(5\times1.6)^2}{2\times2.8} = 11.43\ \mathrm{J}$. Ratio $= \dfrac{14.29}{11.43} = 1.25$, i.e. $1.25:1$. (Check: $E_k = F\,s$ with $s = \tfrac12at^2$ gives the same ratio $\dfrac{t_A^2/m_A}{t_B^2/m_B} = \dfrac{4/3.5}{2.56/2.8} = 1.25$.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The time taken for an object in figure 9 to move from point O to P is;

![fig-9](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: The object is launched at $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal and lands at P at the same height as O. The vertical launch speed is $u_y = 10\sin30^\circ = 5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and the flight time is $$t = \frac{2u_y}{g} = \frac{2\times5.0}{9.81} = 1.0\ \mathrm{s}.$$ (With $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ the result is exactly $1.0\ \mathrm{s}$.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The molar heat capacity of a gas at constant pressure is always greater than that at constant volume because;
questions.corrige_markdown: At constant volume all the heat supplied raises the internal energy. At constant pressure the gas expands, so part of the heat supplied is used to do work $p\,\Delta V$ against the surroundings, and extra heat is needed for the same temperature rise: $C_p = C_V + R$ for an ideal gas. Option B states the resulting difference ($R$), not the reason; D is false (work is done); C is not an explanation. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: at constant pressure, work is done against external pressure in expanding the gas
the molar gas constant makes up the difference between the two heat capacities
at constant volume, the gas does not require much energy to raise the temperature
at constant pressure, no work is done against external pressure

questions.enonce_markdown: At a given instant, five molecules of gas have speeds $100, 200, 250, 300, 600\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ respectively. The root mean square speed of the gas molecules is:
questions.corrige_markdown: $$c_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{100^2 + 200^2 + 250^2 + 300^2 + 600^2}{5}} = \sqrt{\frac{562\,500}{5}} = \sqrt{112\,500} = 335\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$ The mean speed is $290\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is not the rms speed. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A sonometer wire of material of density $5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ is stretched such that transverse waves are transmitted along it at a speed of $160\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The tension per unit area of cross section of the stretched wire is;
questions.corrige_markdown: Wave speed on a string: $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$ with $\mu = \rho A$. Hence $\dfrac{T}{A} = \rho v^2 = (5\times10^{3})(160)^2 = 1.28\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}} \approx 1.3\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. (Only three options, A to C, are printed on the paper.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Sodium light of wavelength $600\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a diffraction grating. If the angle between the first order image and the normal is $17.5^\circ$. The number of lines per millimetre ruled on the grating is:
questions.corrige_markdown: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ with $n = 1$: $d = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}}{\sin17.5^\circ} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}}{0.3007} = 2.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$. Number of lines per metre $= \dfrac{1}{d} = 5.01\times10^{5}$, i.e. $501$ lines per millimetre. Option C is the number per metre. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following methods of power losses in a transformer corresponds to the method of minimizing it?

| | Power loss due to | Minimized by |
|---|---|---|
| A | Heating of wires | Wrapping the primary coil round the secondary |
| B | Poor flux linkage | Using thick copper wires |
| C | Eddy currents | Laminating the transformer core |
| D | Continuous magnetization and demagnetization of core | Using thick wires |
questions.corrige_markdown: Eddy currents are induced in the iron core and waste energy as heat; laminating the core (thin insulated sheets) breaks up their paths and reduces them. The other pairings are mismatched: $I^2R$ heating of the wires is reduced with thick copper wires; poor flux linkage is reduced by winding the secondary over the primary on a closed core; hysteresis loss (repeated magnetization and demagnetization) is reduced by using a soft-iron core. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Heating of wires - wrapping the primary coil round the secondary
Poor flux linkage - using thick copper wires
Eddy currents - laminating the transformer core
Continuous magnetization and demagnetization of core - using thick wires

questions.enonce_markdown: An object is placed $15.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from a converging lens of focal length $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. The image formed is;
questions.corrige_markdown: The object is between $f$ and $2f$. $\dfrac1v = \dfrac1f - \dfrac1u = \dfrac1{10} - \dfrac1{15} = \dfrac1{30}$, so $v = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$ on the other side of the lens (real, inverted). Magnification $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{30}{15} = 2$: the image is twice the height of the object. (Option B is also self-contradictory: an inverted image is not erect.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Electrons drift through a section of a piece of copper wire containing $10^{29}$ electrons per unit volume with a velocity of $2.9\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The current density through the wire is;
The sun emits electromagnetic radiation at the rate of $2.5\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{W}$. The rate at which the sun is losing mass every second is;
questions.corrige_markdown: Energy radiated per second $P = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}c^2$, so $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{P}{c^2} = \dfrac{2.5\times10^{26}}{(3.00\times10^{8})^2} = 2.8\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is **NOT** exhibited by longitudinal waves?
questions.corrige_markdown: Diffraction, refraction and interference are properties of all waves. Polarization requires oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel, so it is exhibited by transverse waves only; the vibrations of a longitudinal wave are along the direction of propagation. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following experimental results of the photoelectric effect can be explained by the classical or wave theory?
questions.corrige_markdown: Wave theory says that a more intense beam carries more energy per second, so more electrons can be released per second: this agrees with experiment. It fails for the others: the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity (A, C), and emission is instantaneous, whereas the wave theory predicts a delay for faint light (D). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The kinetic energy of emitted electrons depending on frequency of incident radiation
Number of photoelectrons emitted per unit time increases with light intensity
Maximum speed of emitted electrons is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation?
The instantaneous emission of electrons from a metal surface even with faint incident radiation

questions.enonce_markdown:
The impedance of the circuit in figure 11 is;

![fig-11](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Capacitive reactance $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\times50\times0.02\times10^{-6}} = 1.59\times10^{5}\ \Omega$. For a series $R$-$C$ circuit, $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + (1.59\times10^{5})^2} \approx 1.59\times10^{5}\ \Omega$ (the $5\ \Omega$ resistance is negligible). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For a fixed mass of gas undergoing an adiabatic change, which of the following is correct?
questions.corrige_markdown: An adiabatic change is one in which no heat enters or leaves the gas. In practice this is achieved by a very fast compression or expansion, so that there is no time for heat transfer, or by thermally insulating the vessel (thick, not thin, walls: C is false). With $Q = 0$, $\Delta U = -W \neq 0$, so the internal energy and the temperature do change (B and D are false). **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The process should be carried out very fast.
There is no change in internal energy of the system
The walls of the containing vessel should be thin.
The initial temperature of the system must necessarily be equal to its final temperature.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 12 shows a couple.

![fig-12](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

The magnitude of the moment of the couple is
questions.corrige_markdown: The two $6\ \mathrm{N}$ forces are horizontal, equal and opposite. The moment of a couple is the force times the perpendicular distance between the lines of action. The bar of length $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$ is inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal, so the perpendicular (vertical) distance between the two horizontal forces is $0.4\sin30^\circ = 0.20\ \mathrm{m}$. $$\text{moment} = 6\times0.20 = 1.2\ \mathrm{N\,m}.$$ Pitfalls: $6\times0.4 = 2.4$ (A) ignores the angle, and $6\times0.4\cos30^\circ = 2.1$ (C) uses the wrong component. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following about capacitors is **NOT** correct?
questions.corrige_markdown: A capacitor passes alternating current (it charges and discharges continuously), stores charge and stores energy $\tfrac12CV^2$. The dielectric between the plates blocks direct current: apart from a brief charging current when it is connected, no steady direct current flows through a capacitor. The statement in D is therefore not correct. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: They allow alternating current to pass through them
Direct current flows through them only in one direction.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following explains why the electrical resistance of metals increases with increase in temperature?
questions.corrige_markdown: In a metal the number of conduction electrons stays practically constant with temperature. As the temperature rises the positive ions of the lattice vibrate with larger amplitude, so conduction electrons collide with them more often and the drift velocity for a given p.d. decreases: resistance increases. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: More positive ions are produced at a higher temperature than conduction electrons.
Electrons do not move fast at higher temperature.
Amplitudes of vibration of positive ions increase with temperature, impeding movement of conduction electrons
Conduction electrons are captured by positive ions at higher temperature.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The force between two small conducting spheres carrying identical charges and placed $4\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart in vacuum is $2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N}$. Which of the following is/are correct?

1. The force is attractive
2. The charge on one of the spheres is $1.9\ \mathrm{nC}$
3. The force is repulsive

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Statements 1 and 3:** identical charges (same sign) repel, so the force is repulsive. 1 is false and 3 is true.

**Statement 2:** $F = \dfrac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$, so $q = \sqrt{\dfrac{F\,r^2}{1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-3})(4\times10^{-3})^2}{8.99\times10^{9}}} = 1.9\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C} = 1.9\ \mathrm{nC}$, so 2 is true.

Statements 2 and 3 are correct. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is/are a difference(s) between stationary and progressive waves?

| | Stationary waves | Progressive waves |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Store energy | Transmit energy |
| 2 | Particles within a given loop vibrate in phase | Particles within a wavelength are not in phase |
| 3 | The wave profile advances with the wave speed | The wave profile does not advance with the wave speed |

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**1 is correct:** a stationary wave stores energy in its loops (no net transfer), while a progressive wave transmits energy.

**2 is correct:** all particles within one loop of a stationary wave vibrate in phase; in a progressive wave the phase changes along one wavelength.

**3 is false as printed:** the columns are interchanged. It is the *progressive* wave whose profile advances with the wave speed, and the *stationary* wave whose profile does not advance.

Only 1 and 2 are correct. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 13 shows the mean distribution of kinetic energy, ke, among a number of molecules N, of a gas at constant temperature $T_1$.

![fig-13](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)

For temperature $T_2 < T_1$, the value of

1. P increases
2. Q decreases
3. P stays constant

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown: The curve is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular kinetic energies. The area under it (total number of molecules) is fixed, and the mean kinetic energy is proportional to $T$. At a lower temperature the distribution shifts to lower energies and becomes narrower and taller. The most probable kinetic energy $Q$ (at the peak, $\approx \tfrac12kT$) therefore decreases and the peak height $P$ increases. Statement 3 is false. Statements 1 and 2 are correct. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Passengers in a moving car jerk-forward when the driver suddenly apply brakes. This is a consequence of ;

1. Newton's third law of motion
2. law of conservation of energy
3. Newton's first law of motion

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown: The car slows down but the passengers tend to keep moving with the same velocity because no force acts on them to stop them: this is inertia, Newton's first law. Newton's third law concerns action-reaction pairs acting on different bodies (not involved here), and conservation of energy does not explain the jerk. Only 3 is correct. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following statements is/are true about fields?

1. Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges
2. A gravitational field is due only to the presence of a charge
3. An electric field is produced only by a fast moving charge

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown: 1 is true: a moving charge (a current) produces a magnetic field. 2 is false: a gravitational field is due to the presence of a mass, not a charge. 3 is false: any charge, even at rest, produces an electric field. Only 1 is correct. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mole of an ideal gas contained in a $0.025$ cubic metre vessel is subjected to a pressure of $10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Which of the following is/are correct?

1. If the pressure of the gas in the same containing vessel is doubled, the temperature of the gas will decrease by half
2. The temperature of the gas is $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
3. The mean kinetic energy of the gas molecule is $6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Statement 1 is false:** at constant volume and amount, $p \propto T$, so doubling the pressure doubles the (kelvin) temperature; it does not halve it.

**Statement 2:** $pV = nRT$ gives $T = \dfrac{pV}{nR} = \dfrac{10^{5}\times0.025}{1\times8.31} = 301\ \mathrm{K} = 27.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. This differs from the printed $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ by $2.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so it is false if taken strictly, but it could be accepted as an approximation ($298\ \mathrm{K}$ against $301\ \mathrm{K}$, a $1\%$ difference).

**Statement 3 is true:** $\overline{E_k} = \tfrac32kT = 1.5\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times301 = 6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

So 3 is correct and 1 is not; the key is either **D** (3 only, strict reading of statement 2) or **B** (2 and 3, if $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is accepted as approximately $301\ \mathrm{K}$). The statement 2 is too borderline to be marked automatically, so the question is left open for self-assessment and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The second law of thermodynamics helps one to understand that;

1. net heat flows only in a particular direction in the universe.
2. the entropy of the universe changes with time.
3. heat does not flow from a cold to hot object naturally.

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
All three statements are accepted consequences of the second law: heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold bodies (1), the total entropy of the universe increases with time in real (irreversible) processes (2), and heat does not flow by itself from a cold to a hot body (Clausius statement, 3). Statements 1 and 3 are in fact two ways of saying the same thing.

The answer "1, 2 and 3 are correct" is not offered: the options only allow two statements at most. Whichever statement the examiner meant to reject (the vague statement 1 or the loose "changes" in statement 2 are the likely candidates), the printed question cannot be marked reliably, so it is left open and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
X-rays are produced when:

1. fast moving electrons strike a metal target and are brought to rest suddenly
2. electrons in discrete higher energy levels in an atom make a transition to the lower energy levels.
3. a metal surface is illuminated with light of appropriate frequency.

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown: 1 is correct: electrons decelerated in a metal target emit a continuous spectrum of X-rays (bremsstrahlung). 2 is correct: when an inner-shell vacancy is filled by an electron falling from a higher level, a photon of a discrete energy is emitted, giving the characteristic X-ray lines. 3 describes the photoelectric effect, which releases electrons, not X-rays. Statements 1 and 2 are correct. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following deduction(s) from the alpha-particle scattering experiment ties with the conclusion?

| | Deduction | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A few $\alpha$-particles were deflected through large angles | The positively charged core occupies a very tiny part of the atom |
| 2 | A very tiny proportion of the $\alpha$-particles bounce back | The atom consists of a positively charged core |
| 3 | Most of the $\alpha$-particles passed through the foil undeflected | The atom consists of mostly empty space |

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
**3 is correct:** most particles pass straight through, so most of the atom is empty space.

**2 is correct:** a very small proportion is turned back through more than $90^\circ$ only by a strong repulsion from a concentrated, massive, positively charged core.

**1 is also acceptable:** large-angle deflections of a few particles show that the positive charge is concentrated in a very small region (in the usual textbook argument it is the small *fraction* deflected that shows the core is tiny).

All three pairings can be defended, and no option offers "1, 2 and 3". Because the key cannot be settled from the printed question, it is left open and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 14 shows the magnetic field that results when a piece of iron is placed between unlike magnetic poles.

![fig-14](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_14.png)

At which point or points is the magnetic field strength strongest?

1. Points B and D
2. Point A
3. Point C

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
The strength of a magnetic field is shown by how close the field lines are. The iron concentrates the lines (high permeability), so the field is strong inside the iron; point A lies outside the iron, above it, where there are almost no field lines, so the field there is weakest (statement 2 is wrong). Point C is inside the iron, where the lines are straight and closely packed. Points B and D are in the gaps between the poles and the iron, where the lines are drawn with almost the same spacing as inside the iron but curve and spread out towards the pole faces.

The best reading of the figure is point C (statement 3, option D), but the sketch is a rough scan and the spacing of the lines at B, C and D is almost the same, so "points B and D" cannot be ruled out with certainty. The question is left open and no letter is designated.

The graphs below are for $y$ = displacement of a body undergoing SHM, and $x$ = acceleration.

![fig-15](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_15.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it: $a = -\omega^2 x_{disp}$. With $y = x_{disp}$ and $x = a$, $y = -\dfrac{1}{\omega^2}x$: a straight line through the origin with a negative gradient. That is graph B. Graph A has a positive gradient, C is a V shape ($y \propto |x|$) and D is an inverted V. **Answer: B.**

The graphs below are for $y$ = the velocity of a train that takes off from rest, at one station and accelerates uniformly before stopping at the next station, and $x$ = time.

![fig-16](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_16.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: Starting from rest with uniform acceleration the velocity rises along a straight line from the origin; it then falls uniformly (uniform deceleration) until the train stops at the next station. The graph is a triangle: graph D. Graph A has a negative velocity branch or does not start from rest, B (parabola) and C (curve levelling off) correspond to non-uniform acceleration. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = voltage across a diode, and $x$ = current through the diode.

![fig-17](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_17.png)

*Options as printed:* A) curve rising steeply from a positive $y$-intercept then levelling off   B) horizontal line (constant $y$)   C) decreasing curve levelling off   D) straight line with a positive $y$-intercept
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a forward-biased diode the current rises exponentially with the voltage, $I = I_0\,e^{eV/kT}$, so the voltage is logarithmic in the current, $V = \dfrac{kT}{e}\ln\dfrac{I}{I_0}$: $V$ rises quickly for small currents and then increases only very slowly. The shape of graph A (rising and levelling off) matches this. Graph B would be the idealised constant forward voltage drop ($\approx 0.6\ \mathrm{V}$ for silicon) once the diode conducts, and graph D is the response of an ohmic resistor; C is decreasing, which no diode does.

The intended answer is probably A, but B can also be argued (constant forward voltage) and the printed graphs are drawn roughly, so the question is left open and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = the square of the velocity of a satellite orbiting the earth, and $x$ = radius of orbit of the satellite.

![fig-18](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_18.png)

*Options as printed:* A) decreasing curve starting at a dotted vertical line (a minimum value of $x$) and levelling off   B) straight line through the origin   C) decreasing curve starting on the $y$-axis and levelling off   D) rising straight line then decreasing curve (peak)
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a circular orbit gravity provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v^2 = \dfrac{GM}{r}$. The graph of $v^2$ against $r$ is a hyperbola: decreasing and approaching the $r$-axis. B (straight line) and D (peak) are therefore wrong.

Both A and C have the decreasing shape. A starts at a dotted line, which can be read as the smallest possible orbit radius (the radius of the earth, since there is no orbit below it); C starts on the $y$-axis, where $r = 0$ and $v^2$ would be infinite. A is physically the more accurate drawing and C the textbook $1/x$ shape, so the key is ambiguous. The question is left open and no letter is designated.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs below are for $y$ = mass of a rocket moving with constant linear momentum, and $x$ = velocity of the rocket.

![fig-19](gce-al-physics-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_19.png)
questions.corrige_markdown: The momentum $p = mv$ is constant, so $m = \dfrac{p}{v}$: the mass is inversely proportional to the velocity, giving a hyperbola that falls steeply for small $v$ and approaches the $v$-axis without touching it. Graph C has this shape. Graph D flattens out at a non-zero value (an exponential-type decay), A (constant) and B (proportional) are wrong. **Answer: C.**
